title: Migrator role's intended trust model is not documented on-chain — natspec describes capabilities but not the assumed role-holder profile
description:
The plan models the migrator (via `MigrationHelper`) as 'no admin, no upgrade path. Holds no funds between txs.' This is a strong claim about the trust model — the role is intended to be a stateless, single-purpose contract whose code can be audited in full before assignment.

The on-chain documentation only says (lines 80-82): 'Address authorised to call `stakeFor`/`unstakeFor` and (jointly with the owner) `withdrawRewardToken`. Settable by owner via `setMigrator`. `address(0)` disables all migrator-gated functions.' This describes WHAT the migrator can do, not WHO the migrator is supposed to be.

A user reading the source code sees a privileged role that can (a) pull NFTs from any beneficiary's stake (line 558), and (b) drain the reward token when paused and `totalStaked == 0` (line 564). There is no on-chain hint that this role is intended to be a stateless, restricted helper. A future deployer (or auditor) cannot derive the trust model from the source alone — this is the inverse of the standard `Ownable` situation, where the trust model is widely understood. The `migrator` role is a project-specific concept with no established norms.

This finding is preserved separately from DEDUP-01 (which addresses the role's *powers* in code) and DEDUP-02 (which addresses *rotation timing*) because the mitigation here is documentation-only — even if DEDUP-01 and DEDUP-02 are fixed, a leaner `migrator` role still benefits from an explicit on-chain statement of its assumed profile.
impact: Documentation drift between off-chain plan and on-chain code. A future deployer following the on-chain documentation alone (without the plan) may set `migrator` to a general admin multisig or EOA, expanding the trust surface beyond what the plan's helper actually requires. The current deployment is presumably correct; the concern is downstream deployments or re-uses of `NFTStakerV2` in other contexts, and the operational risk that a future incident-response rotation re-assigns the role under a different mental model than the original deployment.
recommendation: Expand the natspec on the `migrator` declaration (lines 79-83) and on each migrator-gated function to state the intended trust assumption explicitly. For example: 'In production this role is held by the MigrationHelper contract — a stateless, single-purpose contract with no admin and no upgrade path. Assigning this role to a multisig, EOA, or any contract holding state across calls expands the trust surface beyond the migration plan's design.' Cross-reference the migration plan document or a checked-in design doc so the on-chain reader can locate the full trust model.
attack_scenario: Not directly attackable. The risk is operational/governance: a future deployer following the on-chain documentation alone (without the migration plan) reads `migrator` as a general admin slot and assigns it to a multisig or EOA. That role-holder can then do everything documented above — see DEDUP-01 for the full drain sequence. The current deployment matches the plan; the documentation gap is a footgun for future re-deployments and for future incident-response rotations performed by operators who weren't part of the original design.
